items.q: What makes a hash map's lookup by key fast on average?
options: It stores everything twice for redundancy
A hash function turns the key into a number that points straight to the right bucket
It keeps all keys sorted and binary-searches them
It checks every stored key until it finds a match

explain.right: Hashing the key gives an index into the internal array, so the map jumps straight to the bucket, giving average O(1) lookup.
explain.wrong: It doesn't need sorting or a full scan, and it doesn't duplicate everything; the hash-to-bucket jump is the key idea.

items.q: Hash map lookups are 'O(1)' in which sense?
options: Only if the map has fewer than 100 items
On average; the worst case can degrade toward O(n) when many keys collide
O(1) for reads but O(n) for every write
Always exactly one step, guaranteed, no matter what

explain.right: It's average-case O(1); heavy collisions (many keys in one bucket) can push the worst case toward O(n).
explain.wrong: It isn't a hard guarantee or size-limited, and writes are also average O(1), not O(n).

items.q: A balanced binary search tree can find an item in about O(log n) steps because:
options: Trees are stored contiguously like arrays
Each comparison discards about half the remaining items (go left or right)
It hashes the value to a bucket

explain.right: At each node you go left or right, halving the remaining search space, so a balanced tree takes about log n steps.
explain.wrong: It doesn't visit every node, isn't stored like an array, and doesn't hash; the halving is what gives O(log n).

items.q: Which problem is most naturally a graph problem?
options: Finding the shortest route between two cities connected by roads
Looking up a phone number by a person's exact name
Storing a single sorted list of numbers
Keeping a running total of a counter

explain.right: Cities as nodes and roads as edges is a graph; shortest-path between connected things is a classic graph problem.
explain.wrong: Exact-key lookup suits a hash map, and a sorted list or a counter don't involve arbitrary connections between items.

items.q: Match each to a good use: hash map, tree, graph. Give one use each.
rubric: Hash map: fast lookup of a value by a unique key (e.g. user by id)
Tree: a hierarchy or sorted data searchable by halving (e.g. file system, sorted index)
Graph: modeling relationships/networks and moving between connected things (e.g. social network, maps/routing)

explain.right: Strong answers pair map→key lookup, tree→hierarchy/sorted search, graph→relationships/networks, each with a concrete example.
explain.wrong: A weak answer swaps them (e.g. 'use a graph to look up by key') or gives no example showing the fit.
